query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel’s pre-exposure state, the corrosion resistance at room temperature arises from the formation of a coherent, protective iron-oxide scale that limits further attack. However, when exposed to aggressive salt environments at high temperature (700–900 °C), thermal activation drives phase transformations and accelerates oxide scale coarsening and spallation, thereby degrading the protective layer and leading to accelerated corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with its native microstructure and natural oxide content.
generation.intervention: Expose identical Q235 steel samples to a corrosive salt atmosphere under two controlled temperature regimes: room temperature and 700–900 °C.
generation.conditions: All samples are subjected to the same salt composition, exposure duration, and atmospheric conditions. Temperature is the sole variable. In-situ high-temperature XRD and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) are used to monitor oxide phase evolution and protective properties in real time.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation, phase integrity, and spatial continuity of the iron-based oxide scale (e.g., mixtures of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4) that forms on the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the native oxide rapidly establishes a thin, adherent, and protective barrier that limits ion transport and corrosion. At high temperatures, increased diffusion and thermal stresses promote phase transformations, coarsening, and mechanical spallation of the oxide scale, thereby removing the protective cover and exposing fresh metal for rapid corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to room-temperature tests, high-temperature exposure will yield (a) detectable changes in oxide phase composition by in-situ XRD (e.g., disappearance or transformation of protective phases), (b) lower impedance and higher corrosion current by EIS measurements, and (c) greater mass loss or visually spalled oxide regions post-test.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples exposed to the same corrosive salt environment at room temperature, where the protective oxide scale remains intact and corrosion indicators are minimal.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to Q235 steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) state under the defined salt composition and exposure time. It does not necessarily extend to specimens that have been pre-annealed or modified (e.g., by depositing HEA layers) which might form different oxide scales or rely on additional protective mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The specific oxide phases involved, the exact thermal activation energy for the scale disruption process, and the quantitative rate of corrosion acceleration at high temperatures remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple Q235 steel specimens with the identical pre-exposure microstructure. Expose one set to a corrosive salt environment at room temperature and a second set at 700–900 °C for the same duration. Use in-situ high-temperature XRD to monitor phase changes in the oxide scale and perform electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) during the tests. Post-exposure, assess mass change, oxide spallation, and microstructural integrity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
measurements: Phase identification and transformation of the oxide layer via XRD
Electrochemical impedance measurements to quantify protective behavior
Mass loss measurements to assess corrosion rate
Surface morphology and continuity of oxide scale using SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature specimens show oxide phase characteristics, impedance values, mass loss, and surface morphology that are statistically indistinguishable from those measured at room temperature (i.e., a continuous and adherent oxide scale persists with no significant spallation or increased corrosion rate), then the hypothesis that thermal-induced oxide disruption governs the increased corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study aims to test the effect of the elemental stability inherent in HEAs due to the high configurational entropy and/or sluggish diffusion (if any) on the elemental dissolution in the molten salt. Specifically, the study focuses on corrosion performance and thermal stability of the Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy in molten fluoride salt environment. This multi-component alloy with both Mn and Cr which are reactive in molten fluoride salt is well suited to test these hypotheses. This high entropy alloy was exposed to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours followed by detailed analysis of corrosion in the near-surface regions of the alloy in terms of elemental dissolution into the molten salt and morphological changes at the surface. The results were compared to that of 316 H stainless steel tested under similar conditions.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Thermal stability and applicability to nuclear applications
cited_evidence.text: The use of HEAs in nuclear applications depends greatly on their microstructural stability in the extreme environments of the operating conditions. Although Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy shows good mechanical properties and relatively high resistance to radiation damage, this study showed that the alloy experienced phase instability at 700 °C after 1000 hours. Cr-rich particles were found to precipitate in the alloy, even well beneath the corrosion affected region, after the high temperature exposure during the corrosion test. Just underneath the surface, few fine circular Cr-rich precipitates were observed. As the distance from the surface increased, the Cr-rich precipitates’ concentration increased and their morphology became more needle-shaped as shown in Fig. 6. Then, the precipitates’ concentration decreased significantly but persisted through the entire thickness of the sample as shown in Figs. 6 and 9. These changes in the concentration and morphology of the Cr-rich precipitates indicate that the precipitation process not only depends on both the annealing temperature and duration, but also on the Mn concentration in the alloy, which varies due to its dissolution in the salt.

occupying_moves.technique: in‐situ high‐temperature XRD combined with electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
occupying_moves.conditions: Q235 steel samples with identical pre-exposure microstructure are subjected to controlled corrosive salt environments at room temperature versus 700–900 °C to monitor the evolution and stability of protective oxide phases.

occupying_moves.technique: HEA deposition followed by systematic annealing and hot-corrosion testing
occupying_moves.conditions: Comparison of Q235 steel with and without an added HEA layer under identical hot-corrosion conditions to examine whether annealing-induced microstructural changes modify the corrosion behavior.

chosen.technique: in‐situ high‐temperature XRD combined with electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and post-test microstructural analysis
chosen.conditions: Q235 steel samples (in their pre-exposure state) are tested in a corrosive salt atmosphere at both room temperature and 700–900 °C, while all other variables (chemical composition, sample history, salt type, and exposure duration) are kept constant.
chosen.why: This move most directly addresses the primary unexplained behavior – why corrosion protection persists or fails across low- and high-temperature regimes. By isolating temperature as the sole controlled variable, the study can test the mechanistic hypothesis that the evolution or disruption of protective oxide phases (as evidenced by phase and impedance changes) governs the corrosion outcome. The approach leverages standard in-situ high-temperature characterization methods that are well established within the field.
